idea.e: Borrowed from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”).
idea.g: An abstract archetype of a given thing, compared to which real-life examples are seen as imperfect approximations; pure essence, as opposed

identify.e: From French identifier, from Medieval Latin identicus + Latin faciō.
identify.g: To establish the identity of someone or something.

identity.e: From Middle English ydemptite, from Middle French identité and its etymon Late Latin idemptitās, identitās, from idem (“the same”) + -tās (suffix forming abstract nouns) as a calque of Ancient Greek ταὐτότης (tautótēs, “sameness”).
identity.g: Sameness, identicalness; the quality or fact of (several specified things) being the same.

idle.e: From Middle English idel, ydel, from Old English īdel, from Proto-West Germanic *īdl, from Proto-Germanic *īdlaz. German Low German iedel (“vain, idle”); German eitel (“vain, conceited”); and possibly Old Norse illr ("bad"; > English ill).
From Middle English idelen, from Old English īdlian, from Proto-West Germanic *īdlēn.
idle.g: To spend (time) in idleness; to waste; to consume.

idleness.e: From Middle English ydelnesse, from Old English īdelnes, from Proto-West Germanic *īdlanassī, equivalent to idle + -ness.
idleness.g: The state of being idle; inactivity.

idol.e: From Middle English ydole, from Old French idole, from Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing, image”), from *weyd- (“to see”).
idol.g: A graven image or representation of anything that is revered, or believed to convey spiritual power.

idolater.e: From Middle English ydolatrer, from Middle French idolatre, from Latin idololatra.
idolater.g: One who worships idols; (historical) a pagan.

idolatry.e: From Middle English ydolatrie, from Old French idolatrie, from Ecclesiastical Latin īdōlatrīa, from Late Latin īdōlolatrīa, from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολατρίᾱ (eidōlolatríā, “worship of idols”), back-formation from εἰδωλολάτρης (eidōlolátrēs), from εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “idol”) & λάτρις (látris, “worshipper”) or λατρεύω (latreúō, “to worship”).
